findings.evidence: DOM order is #s3-step3 "Confirm your order", then #s3-step2 "Enter payment details", then #s3-step1 "Choose a plan"; each carries inline style order:3, order:2, order:1 respectively
findings.fix: Reorder the three .step divs in the DOM to match the intended visual sequence (Choose a plan, Enter payment details, Confirm your order) instead of relying on the CSS order property to reorder them visually.
findings.location: #s3-wizard, <div> wizard-steps container, children #s3-step3, #s3-step2, #s3-step1 in that DOM order, lines 47 to 57
findings.violation: The declared CSS order property reverses the visual sequence of the three wizard steps relative to their DOM order, so a linearized reading hears the confirm-and-pay step before the plan-selection step that must happen first, reversing the decision sequence WCAG-1.3.2 requires the DOM order to preserve.

findings.evidence: The page exposes only a two-link primary navigation menu (Plan a trip, Service alerts); no search form, sitemap link, breadcrumb trail, or related-links list appears anywhere in the document, and the page is not marked as one step of a linear process
findings.fix: Add a second independent mechanism, such as a site search form, a sitemap link, or a breadcrumb trail that does not just duplicate the primary navigation's own links.
findings.violation: Fewer than two independent navigation mechanisms are present for a standalone content page, breaching WCAG-2.4.5's requirement that a reader be able to locate the page through more than one mechanism.

findings.evidence: The div wraps only an img with alt="" and carries no role, no aria-label or other accessible name, and no tabindex or other keyboard handling
findings.fix: Mark up the control as a native <button> with a visible or aria-label text name (for example "Delete"), or add role="button", an accessible name, and keyboard handling if it must remain a div.
findings.violation: A custom interactive control built from generic markup exposes no role, no programmatically determinable name, and no keyboard access, breaching WCAG-4.1.2's requirement that every custom component expose its name, role, and state.

findings.evidence: style="color:#cc0000" is the only styling difference between this label and the sibling labels #s3-form-email-label and #s3-form-promo-label, with no asterisk, "required" text, icon, or aria-required attribute on #phone accompanying it
findings.fix: Add a visible non-color indicator (an asterisk plus required text, or an explanatory instruction) alongside the red label, or remove the color if it is not meant to signal anything.
findings.violation: Color alone (red label text) is the only signal distinguishing this field from the others, with no non-color indicator carrying the same information, breaching WCAG-1.4.1's requirement that a second signal accompany any color-coded meaning.

findings.evidence: The heading reads "Accessibility improvements," but the section's own text, #s1-p1 and #s1-p2, describes requesting a fare adjustment and checking real time arrivals by phone, neither of which is an accessibility improvement
findings.fix: Rename the heading to match its actual content (for example, "Fares and real time arrivals"), or move the fare-adjustment and arrival-time paragraphs elsewhere and give the accessible-parking repainting item its own accurately named heading.
findings.violation: The heading's wording misdescribes the content that actually follows it, breaching WCAG-2.4.6's requirement that a heading predict what comes next.

findings.evidence: The heading reads "Weekend service," but the first paragraph under it, #s2-p1, is the same fare-adjustment boilerplate as #s1-p1 and never mentions weekend service, and the following table reports general zone status with no weekend-specific framing
findings.fix: Replace the fare-adjustment paragraph with weekend-specific content, or rename the heading to match what the section actually covers.
findings.violation: The heading's wording misdescribes the content that actually follows it, breaching WCAG-2.4.6's requirement that a heading predict what comes next.

findings.evidence: The error text reads "Error." for the #promo field, which carries aria-invalid="true"
findings.fix: Replace "Error." with specific text naming the field and the problem, for example "Promo code not recognized. Check the code and try again."
findings.violation: The error text is a generic placeholder that names neither the specific field nor the nature of the problem, breaching WCAG-3.3.1's requirement that error text identify the item and describe what is wrong with it.
